notes.definition: Our understanding of genetics developed over about a hundred years, from Gregor Mendel's breeding experiments in the mid-19th century, which showed that characteristics are inherited as 'units' passed on unchanged, to the discovery of the structure of DNA and how genes work in the mid-20th century.
explanation: In the mid-19th century Gregor Mendel, a monk working in Brno (in what is now the Czech Republic), carried out careful breeding experiments on pea plants. He studied characteristics that had two clear forms, such as tall or dwarf stems and round or wrinkled seeds. He crossed plants, collected the seeds, grew the offspring and counted how many showed each form. He used very large numbers of plants, which made his results more reliable.

When Mendel crossed pure-breeding tall plants with pure-breeding dwarf plants, all the offspring were tall. When he bred these offspring together, the dwarf characteristic reappeared in about a quarter of the next generation, giving a ratio of about 3 tall to 1 dwarf. From results like these he concluded that the inheritance of each characteristic is determined by 'units' that are passed on to descendants unchanged. The dwarf unit had not been destroyed or blended; it was hidden in one generation and showed again in the next.

Mendel published his work in 1866, but its importance was not recognised until after his death in 1884. There are several reasons. He published in a little-known journal of a local natural history society, so few scientists read it. He was a monk rather than a well-known scientist. Chromosomes, genes and DNA had not been discovered, so there was no known structure in cells that could explain his units. His mathematical approach to biology was unusual at the time, and many scientists believed that characteristics from the two parents blended together.

In the late 19th century, improved microscopes and stains allowed scientists to observe the behaviour of chromosomes during cell division. In 1900 Mendel's work was rediscovered by other scientists. In the early 20th century it was observed that chromosomes and Mendel's units behaved in similar ways: both come in pairs, one of each pair comes from each parent, and the pairs separate when gametes are made. This led to the idea that the units, now called genes, were located on chromosomes.

In the mid-20th century the structure of DNA was determined (in 1953) and the mechanism of gene function was worked out: the sequence of bases in a gene codes for the sequence of amino acids in a protein. This explained how genes are copied and passed on unchanged and how they control characteristics.

This scientific work by many scientists, each building on the evidence of others, led to the gene theory being developed. It is a good example of how scientific ideas change over time: an idea may be ignored at first, and only accepted when new evidence and new technology make it possible to explain it.
keyFacts: Gregor Mendel carried out breeding experiments on pea plants in the mid-19th century.
Mendel observed that the inheritance of each characteristic is determined by 'units' that are passed on to descendants unchanged.
Mendel's units are now called genes.
Mendel's work was not recognised as important until after his death (1884).
In the late 19th century the behaviour of chromosomes during cell division was observed.
In the early 20th century chromosomes and Mendel's units were seen to behave in similar ways, so genes were thought to be located on chromosomes.
In the mid-20th century the structure of DNA was determined and the mechanism of gene function was worked out.
The gene theory was developed through the work of many scientists.
Crossing pure-breeding tall and dwarf pea plants gave all tall offspring; breeding these gave about 3 tall : 1 dwarf.

keyTerms.definition: Mendel's name for the factors that determine each inherited characteristic, passed on to descendants unchanged. They are now called genes.
A small section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a particular sequence of amino acids to make a specific protein.
A structure in the nucleus made of one long DNA molecule carrying many genes; found in pairs in body cells.
A plant or animal that always produces offspring with the same characteristic when bred with a similar individual (homozygous).
Describes a characteristic or allele that shows whenever it is present, such as tall stems in Mendel's peas.
Describes a characteristic or allele that only shows when no dominant allele is present, such as dwarf stems in Mendel's peas.
The theory that characteristics are controlled by genes, which are sections of DNA on chromosomes passed from parents to offspring.

workedExamples.title: Calculating a ratio from Mendel's data
workedExamples.question: In one experiment Mendel counted 5474 plants with round seeds and 1850 plants with wrinkled seeds. Calculate the ratio of round to wrinkled in the form x : 1. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
steps: To get a ratio in the form x : 1, divide both numbers by the smaller number.
Round to 2 decimal places: 2.96 : 1, which is very close to 3 : 1.

workedExamples.title: Explaining Mendel's tall and dwarf results with units
workedExamples.question: Mendel crossed pure-breeding tall pea plants with pure-breeding dwarf pea plants. All offspring were tall. When these offspring were bred together, 787 were tall and 277 were dwarf. Explain these results using Mendel's idea of units.
steps: Use T for the tall unit (dominant) and t for the dwarf unit (recessive). Pure-breeding tall = TT, pure-breeding dwarf = tt.
Each parent passes on one unit: TT gives T, tt gives t, so all offspring are Tt and look tall because T is dominant.
Breeding Tt × Tt: each parent passes on T or t. Offspring are TT, Tt, Tt and tt.
Three of the four combinations contain T, so are tall; one (tt) is dwarf. Expected ratio 3 tall : 1 dwarf.
787 ÷ 277 = 2.84, so the results are close to 3 : 1. The dwarf unit was passed on unchanged through the tall generation.
workedExamples.answer: Units are passed on unchanged; tall is dominant over dwarf, so the first generation is all tall (Tt) and the second generation shows about 3 tall : 1 dwarf.

workedExamples.title: Working out time spans in the history of genetics
workedExamples.question: Mendel published his results in 1866 and his work was rediscovered in 1900. The structure of DNA was determined in 1953. How many years passed between Mendel's publication and (a) its rediscovery, (b) the discovery of DNA structure?

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think Mendel knew about genes, chromosomes and DNA.
misconceptions.right: In fact, Mendel only described 'units' of inheritance. Chromosomes, genes and DNA were described by later scientists, which is one reason his work was ignored at first.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think Mendel's work was ignored because his results were wrong.
misconceptions.right: In fact, his results were accurate. His work was overlooked because it was published in a little-known journal, he was not a well-known scientist, and no one could explain the units at the time.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think characteristics from two parents blend together in the offspring.
misconceptions.right: In fact, Mendel showed that units are passed on unchanged: dwarf plants reappeared in the second generation, so the dwarf unit had not been blended away.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think one scientist discovered the gene theory.
misconceptions.right: In fact, the gene theory was developed by many scientists over about 100 years, each building on earlier evidence.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a 3 : 1 ratio means the numbers will be exactly three times as many.
misconceptions.right: In fact, it is an expected ratio based on probability. Real counts, such as 787 : 277, are close to 3 : 1 but not exact.

realWorld: Mendel's ideas about dominant and recessive units underpin genetic counselling, where the chance of a child inheriting a disorder such as cystic fibrosis is worked out.
Plant and animal breeders use Mendel's rules to predict the characteristics of offspring when developing new crop varieties.
The discovery of DNA structure led to modern technologies such as genetic testing and genome sequencing.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Biology only (not Combined Science Trilogy): the work of Mendel, why its importance was not recognised until after his death, and the development of the gene theory from chromosome observations to the structure of DNA.
examTips: Learn the sequence by century: mid-19th (Mendel), late 19th (chromosomes in cell division), early 20th (units on chromosomes, called genes), mid-20th (DNA structure and gene function).
For 'why was Mendel's work not recognised', give separate, specific reasons: little-known journal, not a well-known scientist, genes/chromosomes/DNA not yet known.
Use Mendel's own word 'units' when describing his observations, then link it to the modern word 'genes'.
When calculating a ratio in the form x : 1, divide both numbers by the smaller number.
In questions on how science develops, say that new evidence and new technology (such as better microscopes) allowed ideas to be tested and accepted.
summary: Mendel bred pea plants in the mid-19th century and found that characteristics are inherited as units passed on unchanged.
His work was not recognised until after his death, partly because genes, chromosomes and DNA were unknown.
Late 19th century: the behaviour of chromosomes during cell division was observed.
Early 20th century: chromosomes and units behave alike, so genes are on chromosomes.
Mid-20th century: the structure of DNA and how genes work were discovered.
Many scientists contributed to the gene theory.

questions.question: Which organisms did Gregor Mendel use in his breeding experiments?
markScheme: 1 mark: pea plants
questions.explanation: Mendel bred pea plants. Fruit flies were used later, in the early 20th century, to show genes are on chromosomes; bacteria and mice were not part of Mendel's work.

questions.question: When did Mendel carry out his breeding experiments?
markScheme: 1 mark: mid-19th century
questions.explanation: Mendel worked in the mid-19th century (he published in 1866). The early 20th century is when genes were linked to chromosomes, and the mid-20th century is when DNA's structure was found.

questions.question: What did Mendel conclude determines the inheritance of each characteristic?
options: Units that are passed on to descendants unchanged
Characteristics gained during the parents' lifetime
markScheme: 1 mark: units that are passed on to descendants unchanged
questions.explanation: Mendel's key observation was that characteristics are controlled by units passed on unchanged. Blending and inheritance of acquired characteristics were older, incorrect ideas, and DNA's structure was not known until 1953.

questions.question: What are Mendel's 'units' of inheritance called today?
markScheme: 1 mark: genes
questions.explanation: Mendel's units are now called genes. Chromosomes carry many genes, gametes are sex cells and nuclei contain the chromosomes.

questions.question: What did scientists observe in the late 19th century that later helped to explain Mendel's work?
options: The double helix structure of DNA
The behaviour of chromosomes during cell division
The order of all the genes in human DNA
markScheme: 1 mark: the behaviour of chromosomes during cell division
questions.explanation: Better microscopes and stains let scientists see chromosomes during cell division in the late 19th century. DNA structure came in the mid-20th century and whole genome sequencing much later.

questions.question: In the early 20th century, which observation led scientists to suggest that genes are located on chromosomes?
options: Chromosomes were found to be made of protein only
Mendel's units could be seen with a microscope
Chromosomes and Mendel's units were seen to behave in similar ways
Every chromosome was found to carry only one gene
markScheme: 1 mark: chromosomes and Mendel's units behaved in similar ways
questions.explanation: Both chromosomes and units come in pairs and separate when gametes form, so scientists linked them. Units could not be seen directly, chromosomes carry many genes, and they contain DNA as well as protein.

questions.question: In which year was the structure of DNA determined?
markScheme: 1 mark: 1953
questions.explanation: The structure of DNA was determined in 1953, in the mid-20th century. 1866 is when Mendel published, 1900 is when his work was rediscovered, and 2003 is when the Human Genome Project was completed.

questions.question: Which is a reason why the importance of Mendel's work was not recognised during his lifetime?
options: His results did not fit a 3 : 1 ratio
He only used a very small number of plants
Other scientists repeated his work and got the same results
Chromosomes, genes and DNA had not yet been discovered
markScheme: 1 mark: chromosomes, genes and DNA had not yet been discovered
questions.explanation: Without knowledge of chromosomes, genes or DNA, there was nothing to explain his units. His results did fit 3 : 1, he used thousands of plants, and repeated results would have helped, not hindered, acceptance.

questions.question: Mendel crossed pure-breeding tall pea plants with pure-breeding dwarf pea plants. What were the offspring like?
markScheme: 1 mark: all tall
questions.explanation: Tall is dominant, so every offspring (Tt) was tall. 'All medium height' is what blending inheritance would predict, and Mendel's results showed this idea was wrong.

questions.question: Mendel crossed pure-breeding tall pea plants with pure-breeding dwarf pea plants, and all the offspring were tall. He then bred these tall offspring with each other. Which ratio did he observe in the next generation?
markScheme: 1 mark: 3 tall : 1 dwarf
questions.explanation: Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt: three tall to one dwarf. 1 : 1 comes from Tt × tt, and 1 tall : 3 dwarf has the dominant and recessive the wrong way round.

questions.question: Which statement best describes how the gene theory was developed?
options: Mendel discovered genes, chromosomes and DNA in one series of experiments
It was accepted immediately in 1866 because Mendel's evidence was so strong
It was developed in 1953 when DNA was discovered, without using earlier work
Many scientists contributed over about 100 years, each building on earlier evidence
markScheme: 1 mark: many scientists contributed over about 100 years, building on earlier evidence
questions.explanation: The gene theory grew from Mendel's units, observations of chromosomes, the link between the two, and finally DNA structure. Mendel's work was not accepted immediately, and 1953 built on all the earlier work.

questions.question: Mendel published his work in 1866. He died in 1884. Calculate how many years he lived after publishing his work.
questions.explanation: 1884 − 1866 = 18 years. During all this time the importance of his work was not recognised.

questions.question: In one experiment Mendel grew 787 tall plants and 277 dwarf plants. Calculate the percentage of plants that were tall. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation: First find the total: 1064 plants. Then 787 ÷ 1064 × 100 = 73.97%, which rounds to 74%. This is close to the 75% expected from a 3 : 1 ratio.

questions.question: In another experiment Mendel counted 5474 plants with round seeds and 1850 plants with wrinkled seeds. Calculate the ratio of round to wrinkled seeds in the form x : 1. Give x to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Divide both numbers by the smaller one: 5474 ÷ 1850 = 2.9589..., which is 2.96 to 2 decimal places, so the ratio is 2.96 : 1. This is very close to Mendel's expected 3 : 1.

questions.question: Mendel grew 1064 plants from a cross where the expected ratio was 3 tall : 1 dwarf. Calculate the number of dwarf plants expected.
markScheme: 1 mark: dwarf = 1 out of 4 parts / 1064 ÷ 4
1 mark: 266
questions.explanation: A 3 : 1 ratio has 4 parts in total, and dwarf is 1 part. 1064 ÷ 4 = 266. Mendel actually counted 277, close to the expected value.

questions.question: Mendel's work was published in 1866 and rediscovered by other scientists in 1900. Calculate how many years passed between publication and rediscovery.
questions.explanation: 1900 − 1866 = 34 years. Mendel had already died in 1884, so he never saw his work recognised.

questions.question: Name the scientist who carried out breeding experiments on plants in the mid-19th century and suggested that characteristics are inherited as 'units'.
markScheme: 1 mark: (Gregor) Mendel
questions.explanation: Gregor Mendel was a monk who bred pea plants. Do not confuse him with Darwin or Wallace, who proposed natural selection.

questions.question: Describe one of Mendel's main observations about inheritance.
markScheme: 1 mark: the inheritance of each characteristic is determined by units
1 mark: which are passed on to descendants unchanged
questions.explanation: Mendel's key idea was that each characteristic is controlled by units passed on unchanged, not blended. Both parts are needed for 2 marks.

questions.question: State what scientists observed about chromosomes in the late 19th century.
acceptedAnswers: behaviour of chromosomes during cell division
how chromosomes behave when cells divide
markScheme: 1 mark: the behaviour of chromosomes during cell division
questions.explanation: Improved microscopes allowed scientists to watch chromosomes during cell division in the late 19th century.

questions.question: When Mendel crossed tall and dwarf pea plants, the dwarf characteristic disappeared in the first generation but reappeared in the second generation. Explain how this supports the idea that units are passed on unchanged.
markScheme: 1 mark: the dwarf unit was still present in the first generation but hidden (by the dominant tall unit)
1 mark: it was passed on unchanged / not blended, so it showed again when a plant inherited two dwarf units
questions.explanation: If characteristics blended, the dwarf unit would have been lost. Its reappearance shows it was carried, unchanged, through the tall generation.

questions.question: Give three reasons why the importance of Mendel's work was not recognised until after his death.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any three: published in a little-known / obscure journal; he was a monk / not a well-known scientist; chromosomes, genes and DNA had not been discovered so there was no mechanism for his units; his mathematical approach was unusual in biology; most scientists believed in blending inheritance
questions.explanation: Each reason needs to be specific. 'People did not believe him' is too vague; say why, for example that there was no known structure in cells to explain his units.

questions.question: Explain why the observation that chromosomes and Mendel's units behaved in similar ways led to the idea that genes are on chromosomes.
markScheme: 1 mark: both chromosomes and units occur in pairs / one of each pair comes from each parent
1 mark: both pairs separate so that each gamete gets one, so scientists concluded the units were carried on chromosomes
questions.explanation: Because the patterns matched so closely, scientists inferred that the units (genes) must be located on chromosomes.

questions.question: Explain why the gene theory is described as the result of work by many scientists rather than one.
markScheme: 1 mark: different scientists made different discoveries (e.g. Mendel's units, chromosome behaviour, DNA structure)
1 mark: each built on earlier evidence over a long period (about 100 years)
questions.explanation: No single person could have developed the theory: it needed Mendel's breeding results, chromosome observations, the link between them and the structure of DNA.

questions.question: Mendel used thousands of plants in each experiment. Suggest why this made his conclusions more convincing.
markScheme: 1 mark: a large sample reduces the effect of chance / anomalous results
1 mark: so the ratios are closer to the true / expected ratio (e.g. 3 : 1) and the results are more reliable / repeatable
questions.explanation: Inheritance involves chance. With only a few plants the ratio could be far from 3 : 1 by luck; with thousands, chance effects even out.

questions.question: Explain how the discoveries of the mid-20th century completed our understanding of how Mendel's units work.
markScheme: 1 mark: the structure of DNA was determined (1953)
1 mark: genes were shown to be sections of DNA / the mechanism of gene function was worked out
1 mark: the sequence of bases codes for the sequence of amino acids in a protein, which controls a characteristic / DNA can be copied so genes are passed on unchanged
questions.explanation: Mendel showed what happens; DNA structure explained how. Genes are DNA base sequences that code for proteins, and DNA copying explains why units are passed on unchanged.

questions.question: Describe how scientists' understanding of genetics developed from the mid-19th century to the mid-20th century.
markScheme: Indicative content: mid-19th century, Mendel's breeding experiments on pea plants; he observed that each characteristic is determined by units passed on unchanged; late 19th century, the behaviour of chromosomes during cell division was observed; Mendel's work rediscovered (1900); early 20th century, chromosomes and Mendel's units seen to behave in similar ways; so units (genes) are located on chromosomes; mid-20th century, structure of DNA determined (1953) and mechanism of gene function worked out; work of many scientists led to the gene theory.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear, chronological description covering at least three of the four stages with correct detail.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant stages described, possibly out of order.
questions.explanation: Organise your answer by time period. Each stage builds on the one before: units, then chromosomes, then genes on chromosomes, then DNA.

questions.question: Mendel's work was not recognised as important until after his death. Explain why, and describe how later discoveries showed that his ideas were correct.
markScheme: Indicative content. Why not recognised: published in a little-known journal (of a local natural history society) so few scientists read it; Mendel was a monk / not a well-known scientist; chromosomes, genes and DNA were not known, so there was no mechanism to explain his units; his mathematical / statistical approach was unusual for biology; most scientists believed in blending inheritance. Later discoveries: late 19th century the behaviour of chromosomes in cell division was observed; his work was rediscovered (1900); early 20th century chromosomes and units seen to behave in similar ways (in pairs, separating into gametes), so units (genes) are on chromosomes; mid-20th century structure of DNA determined and how genes work explained, showing how units are copied and passed on unchanged; gene theory developed by many scientists.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed explanation of at least two reasons for non-recognition, linked to a clear, ordered account of later discoveries that provided a mechanism for his units.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some reasons and some later discoveries, with limited linking.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about Mendel or later discoveries, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: The best answers link the two halves: a key reason the work was ignored was the lack of a mechanism, and later discoveries (chromosomes, genes, DNA) provided exactly that mechanism.

questions.question:
Mendel crossed pure-breeding plants with round seeds with pure-breeding plants with wrinkled seeds. All the offspring had round seeds. When these offspring were bred together, the next generation contained 5474 plants with round seeds and 1850 with wrinkled seeds.
Use Mendel's idea of units to explain these results. You may use a genetic diagram.
markScheme: Indicative content: round unit is dominant (R), wrinkled is recessive (r); pure-breeding parents are RR and rr; each parent passes on one unit, so first generation are all Rr and have round seeds; Rr × Rr gives RR, Rr, Rr, rr; expected ratio 3 round : 1 wrinkled; 5474 ÷ 1850 = 2.96, which is close to 3 : 1; the wrinkled unit was passed on unchanged through the first generation.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a correct genetic explanation of both generations, linked to the 3 : 1 ratio and the data.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): partial explanation, e.g. identifies round as dominant or states the expected ratio without explanation.
questions.explanation: Assign symbols, show the gametes from each cross, and finish by comparing the expected 3 : 1 ratio with the real data (2.96 : 1).
